facts.statement: Camarasaurus lived during the Late Jurassic, specifically from the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian ages, between 155 and 143 million years ago.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic, Kimmeridgian to Tithonian, 155–143 Ma

facts.statement: The genus Camarasaurus was described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877.
facts.quote: authority: Cope, 1877

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Camarasaurus is Camarasaurus supremus.
facts.quote: type_species: Camarasaurus supremus

facts.statement: The type species Camarasaurus supremus was named by Cope in 1877.
facts.quote: type_species_authority: Cope, 1877

facts.statement: Other recognized species of Camarasaurus include C. grandis (named by Marsh in 1877), C. lentus (named by Marsh in 1889), and C. lewisi (named by Jensen in 1988).
facts.quote: subdivision: *Camarasaurus grandis (Marsh, 1877) Camarasaurus lentus (Marsh, 1889) Camarasaurus lewisi (Jensen, 1988)

facts.statement: Over 530 specimens of Camarasaurus have been found in the Morrison Formation in the western United States.
facts.quote: Over 530 specimens have been found in rocks of the Morrison Formation in the western United States

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was a bulky sauropod characterized by a proportionally wide rib cage.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus was a bulky sauropod with a proportionally wide rib cage.

facts.statement: The skull of Camarasaurus was proportionally larger and more robust than other sauropods, featuring powerful jaws capable of high bite forces.
facts.quote: Its skull was proportionally larger and more strongly built than that of other sauropods, with powerful jaws that allowed for high bite forces.

facts.statement: The teeth of Camarasaurus were spoon-shaped, tilted forward, and rapidly replaced.
facts.quote: The teeth were spoon-shaped, tilted forwards, and rapidly replaced.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was likely a selective feeder that browsed at heights ranging from 2 to 5 meters.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus was probably a selective feeder that fed at heights of 2 to 5 m.

facts.statement: Skin impressions have been found on at least one specimen of Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Skin impressions have been found on one specimen

facts.statement: Several Camarasaurus specimens show evidence of injury or disease, including bite marks and arthritis.
facts.quote: several specimens show signs of injury or disease, such as bite marks and arthritis

facts.statement: The genus Camarasaurus was named in 1877 by Edward Drinker Cope based on fossils discovered in Garden Park, Colorado.
facts.quote: The genus was named in 1877 by Edward Drinker Cope, based on fossils from Garden Park, Colorado.

facts.statement: Shortly after Cope's discovery, his rival Othniel Charles Marsh named the genus Morosaurus based on specimens from Como Bluff, Wyoming.
facts.quote: Soon after, Cope's rival Othniel Charles Marsh named the new genus Morosaurus from specimens found in Como Bluff, Wyoming.

facts.statement: The genus Morosaurus and its species were later reassigned to the genus Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Morosaurus and its species were later assigned to Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: Since 1909, several largely complete skeletons of Camarasaurus have been discovered in the Carnegie Quarry at Dinosaur National Monument.
facts.quote: From 1909, several largely complete skeletons have been discovered in Carnegie Quarry at what is now Dinosaur National Monument

facts.statement: Camarasaurus is classified as a member of the sauropod group Macronaria.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus is a member of the group Macronaria.

facts.statement: Some paleontologists have debated grouping Camarasaurus with genera like Tehuelchesaurus and Lourinhasaurus in the family Camarasauridae.
facts.quote: Some paleontologists have grouped Camarasaurus with genera like Tehuelchesaurus and Lourinhasaurus in the family Camarasauridae.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was discovered during the 'Bone Wars', a rivalry between paleontologists Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus was discovered during the Bone Wars, a feud between two American paleontologists, Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope

facts.statement: In early 1877, David Baldwin, a collector for Marsh, discovered large bones at Garden Park, Colorado.
facts.quote: In early 1877, David Baldwin, one of Marsh's fossil collectors, discovered very large bones at Garden Park, Colorado

facts.statement: Lucas contacted Cope, who offered payment for excavating the fossils.
facts.quote: Lucas then wrote to Cope, who offered him payment for excavating the fossils.

facts.statement: Cope named the fossils Camarasaurus supremus in a publication in 1877.
facts.quote: Cope gave these fossils the name Camarasaurus supremus in another quickly written 1877 publication.

facts.statement: Lucas and his brother Ira H. Lucas continued sending fossils to Cope until 1884.
facts.quote: Lucas and his brother, Ira H. Lucas, continued to send fossils to Cope until 1884

facts.statement: Cope assigned a set of ten teeth found with the Camarasaurus material to a new genus, Caulodon, in 1877.
facts.quote: Also amongst this material was a set of ten teeth, which Cope assigned to a new genus, Caulodon (meaning stalk tooth), in 1877.

facts.statement: The genus Caulodon is now considered a synonym of Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Caulodon is now thought to be a synonym of Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: The 68-foot-long drawing was based on known Camarasaurus bones and the reconstructed limbs of Morosaurus grandis.
facts.quote: The drawing was 68 ft long and was based on known Camarasaurus bones, as well as the reconstructed limbs of Morosaurus grandis

facts.statement: This drawing is considered the first skeletal reconstruction of a sauropod.
facts.quote: This drawing is the first skeletal reconstruction of a sauropod

facts.statement: Little was known about the Camarasaurus skull at the time, leading researchers to assume it was carnivorous like most extant reptiles.
facts.quote: Little was known of the skull at the time, and since most extant reptiles are carnivorous, it was assumed that the same applied to Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: Consequently, the hypothetical skull in the early reconstruction bore long, sharp teeth.
facts.quote: Consequently, the hypothetical skull bore long, sharp teeth.

facts.statement: William Harlow Reed discovered fossil bones of Camarasaurus on a hill south of Como Station, Wyoming, on March 7, 1877.
facts.quote: On March 7, 1877, at roughly the same time when Lucas began collecting Camarasaurus bones at Garden Park, the railway employee William Harlow Reed found fossil bones on a hill south of Como Station, Wyoming.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh described the first shipment of bones, cataloged as YPM 1901, as a new species of Apatosaurus named A. grandis in December 1877.
facts.quote: In December 1877, Marsh described the bones of the first shipment (later cataloged as YPM 1901) as a new species of his previously established genus Apatosaurus, A. grandis.

facts.statement: Marsh named the species Morosaurus lentus in 1889 based on a nearly complete skeleton without a skull found at Como Bluff.
facts.quote: In 1889, Marsh named the new species Morosaurus lentus based on a nearly complete skeleton without skull found in the "stegosaur" quarry at Como Bluff.

facts.statement: An American Museum of Natural History team led by Walter Granger and Peter Kaisen began excavations at Bone Cabin Quarry in 1898.
facts.quote: In 1898, an AMNH team led by Walter Granger and Peter Kaisen began working at Bone Cabin Quarry, a newly discovered locality just north of Como Bluff.

facts.statement: Bone Cabin Quarry yielded the first nearly complete skull of Camarasaurus, cataloged as FR 467, found connected to neck vertebrae.
facts.quote: The quarry also yielded skulls of several dinosaurs, including the first nearly complete skull of Camarasaurus (FR 467), found connected to a sequence of neck vertebrae.

facts.statement: Earl Douglass discovered Carnegie Quarry in what is now Dinosaur National Monument near Jensen, Utah, in 1909.
facts.quote: In 1909, Earl Douglass of the Carnegie Museum discovered Carnegie Quarry, in what is now Dinosaur National Monument near Jensen, Utah.

facts.statement: Earl Douglass excavated a fully articulated juvenile Camarasaurus skeleton, cataloged as CM 11338, in 1919 and 1920, which remains one of the most complete sauropod skeletons known as of 2021.
facts.quote: In 1919 and 1920, Douglass excavated the fully articulated skeleton of a juvenile (CM 11338), which is, as of 2021, still regarded as one of the most complete sauropod skeletons ever discovered.

facts.statement: William Jacob Holland described the genus Uintasaurus in 1924 based on cervical vertebrae from Carnegie Quarry, but it is now considered a synonym of Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: In 1924, Carnegie Museum's director William Jacob Holland described the new genus Uintasaurus (after Uintah County, Utah) based on five cervical vertebrae from Carnegie Quarry; this genus is now considered as a synonym of Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: The skull DINO 28 was discovered with a fragmentary skeleton in Carnegie Quarry in 1955.
facts.quote: In 1955, the skull DINO 28 was discovered together with a fragmentary skeleton in the Carnegie Quarry.

facts.statement: Historically, the Brontosaurus mount at Yale Peabody Museum and the Apatosaurus mount at the Field Museum were given skulls modeled after or cast from Camarasaurus in 1931 and 1958, respectively.
facts.quote: The skull of the Brontosaurus mount at the Yale Peabody Museum was roughly modeled after Camarasaurus in 1931, and the Apatosaurus mount at the Field Museum was given a cast Camarasaurus skull in 1958.

facts.statement: James A. Jensen collected a two-thirds complete articulated skeleton of Camarasaurus without a skull, cataloged as BYU 9740, from the Uncompahgre Plateau in 1967.
facts.quote: In 1967, James A. Jensen collected an articulated skeleton (BYU 9740) from the Uncompahgre Plateau in western Colorado; this skeleton was two-thirds complete but without skull.

facts.statement: A 65% complete skeleton of Camarasaurus grandis was collected near Bone Cabin Quarry in 1992 by Jeffrie Parker and his team.
facts.quote: In 1992, a 65% complete skeleton of C. grandis was collected by the fossil hunter Jeffrie Parker and team from near Bone Cabin Quarry.

facts.statement: A Swiss team from the Sauriermuseum Aathal found a well-preserved Camarasaurus specimen at Howe-Stephens Quarry in Wyoming in 1992.
facts.quote: Another well-preserved Camarasaurus specimen was found in 1992 at the Howe-Stephens Quarry in Wyoming by a Swiss collecting team of the Sauriermuseum Aathal.

facts.statement: An incomplete skull and skeleton of Camarasaurus from the Little Snowy Mountains of Montana, cataloged as GPDM 220, was described in 2017 as the northernmost known specimen.
facts.quote: In 2017, the hitherto northernmost specimen, an incomplete skull with skeleton (GPDM 220) from the Little Snowy Mountains of Montana, was described.

facts.statement: Mook formally synonymized the genera Morosaurus and Camarasaurus in 1914.
facts.quote: In 1914, Mook formally synonymized the two genera.

facts.statement: John Stanton McIntosh and colleagues determined in 1996 that Cathetosaurus lewisi is a species of Camarasaurus, a view supported by most later studies.
facts.quote: In 1996, John Stanton McIntosh and colleagues determined that Cathetosaurus lewisi was a distinct species of Camarasaurus, as its differences from other Camarasaurus species were not general enough to warrant a separate genus; this opinion was supported by most later studies.

facts.statement: Marsh suggested in 1878 that Morosaurus was very sluggish in movement and had a brain proportionately smaller than any known vertebrate.
facts.quote: Later in 1878, Marsh wrote that his Morosaurus "must have been very sluggish in all its movements", and that "its brain was proportionately smaller than in any known vertebrate".

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn implied in 1898 that Atlantosaurus, Apatosaurus, Amphicoelias, and Brontosaurus were synonyms of Cope's Camarasaurus, a hypothesis that remains a subject of historical debate.
facts.quote: In 1898, Henry Fairfield Osborn, who despised Marsh, even implied that the genera Atlantosaurus, Apatosaurus, Amphicoelias, and Brontosaurus were all synonyms of Cope's Camarasaurus, which would have priority as it was named first.

facts.statement: From 1901, papers suggested that Morosaurus and Camarasaurus might be the same genus, leading to their formal synonymization in 1914.
facts.quote: From 1901, several papers suggested that Morosaurus and Camarasaurus might be the same genus, and in 1914, Mook formally synonymized the two genera.

facts.statement: Compared to other sauropods, Camarasaurus was relatively bulky with a wide ribcage.
facts.quote: Compared to other sauropods, it was relatively bulky with a wide ribcage.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was a medium to large-sized sauropod.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus was a medium to large-sized sauropod.

facts.statement: If its body proportions were identical to smaller species, C. supremus would have reached almost 23 meters in length and 42.3 tonnes in weight.
facts.quote: Although C. supremus is too incompletely known to allow for precise size estimates, it would have reached almost 23 m in length and 42.3 t in weight if its body proportions were identical to those of the smaller species.

facts.statement: In 2024, Gregory S. Paul estimated C. supremus to be 18 meters long and weigh 24 tonnes.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul, in 2024, instead gave a length estimate of 18 m and a weight estimate of 24 t for this species.

facts.statement: When viewed from the back, the Camarasaurus skull was almost rectangular and higher than wide.
facts.quote: The skull was almost rectangular when viewed from the back and higher than wide.

facts.statement: The Camarasaurus orbit contained a scleral ring made of small plate-like bones around the pupil.
facts.quote: The orbit contained a scleral ring, a ring of small plate-like bones around the pupil of the eye.

facts.statement: A 2004 review identified four autapomorphies in the Camarasaurus skull not found in related genera.
facts.quote: According to a 2004 review, the skull showed four autapomorphies (anatomical features not found in related genera)

facts.statement: Specimens had four teeth in each premaxilla, 9 to 10 in each maxilla, and 13 in each lower jaw.
facts.quote: Specimens had four teeth in each premaxilla (the front bone of the upper jaw), 9 to 10 teeth in each maxilla (the main bone of the upper jaw), and 13 teeth in each lower jaw.

facts.statement: The vertebral column consisted of 12 cervical, 12 dorsal, and five sacral vertebrae.
facts.quote: The vertebral column consisted of 12 cervical (neck), 12 dorsal (back), and five sacral (hip) vertebrae.

facts.statement: The two specimens preserving complete tails each have 53 caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: The two specimens that preserve a complete tail (CM 11338 and GMNH 101) each have 53 caudal vertebrae.

facts.statement: The cervical and dorsal vertebrae were opisthocoelous and had large side excavations called pleurocoels.
facts.quote: The cervical and dorsal vertebrae were opisthocoelous (concave at the rear and convex at the front) and had large excavations on their sides called pleurocoels.

facts.statement: The humerus was about 77% the length of the femur.
facts.quote: The forelimb was slender, and the humerus was about 77% the length of the femur.

facts.statement: The hindlimb was massive, with the tibia about 60% the length of the femur.
facts.quote: In contrast, the hindlimb was massive, and the tibia (shin bone) was about 60% the length of the femur.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus is one of few sauropods preserving the wrist, which consisted of only two bones.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus is one of few sauropods that preserve the wrist, which in this genus consisted of only two bones.

facts.statement: The thumb consisted of two phalanges including a large, hook-shaped claw slanted sideways.
facts.quote: The fingers were strongly reduced, with the thumb consisting of two phalanges (finger bones), including a large, hook-shaped claw that was slanted sidewards.

facts.statement: Skin impressions on the hind limbs of specimen "E.T." show hexagonal scales between 6 and 18 mm in diameter.
facts.quote: Patches of skin impressions are also preserved on the hind limbs of "E.T.", where they mostly show hexagonal scales that were between 6 and 18 mm in diameter.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope described the genus Camarasaurus in 1877.
facts.quote: In 1877, Cope described Camarasaurus as a new genus of dinosaur

facts.statement: The genus Morosaurus and its family Morosauridae are now considered synonyms of Camarasaurus and the family Camarasauridae.
facts.quote: Marsh later classified Morosaurus in a sauropod family of its own, Morosauridae. Morosaurus and Morosauridae have since been synonymized with Camarasaurus and Camarasauridae, respectively

facts.statement: Since 1998, Camarasaurus has generally been classified as a basal member of the sauropod group Macronaria.
facts.quote: Since 1998, Camarasaurus is generally classified as a basal (early diverging) member of the sauropod group Macronaria.

facts.statement: Four species are commonly recognized within the genus Camarasaurus: C. supremus, C. grandis, C. lentus, and C. lewisi.
facts.quote: Four species are commonly recognized: C. supremus, C. grandis, C. lentus, and C. lewisi.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus lewisi was originally described as the genus Cathetosaurus in 1988 but was reclassified as a species of Camarasaurus in 1996.
facts.quote: C. lewisi was originally described as a distinct genus, Cathetosaurus, in 1988, but reclassified as a species of Camarasaurus in 1996.

facts.statement: It is debated whether C. lentus is a distinct species, as its holotype is a juvenile found in the same locality as C. grandis and lacks diagnostic features.
facts.quote: However, he also noted that the holotype specimen of C. lentus is a juvenile specimen and therefore does not show diagnostic features. Since this specimen was found in Como Bluff, from which C. grandis is known, it might be another example of the latter species.

facts.statement: C. grandis lived during the Kimmeridgian, C. lentus during the late Kimmeridgian, and C. supremus during the Tithonian.
facts.quote: The oldest species, C. grandis, would have occurred during the Kimmeridgian and was followed by C. lentus in the late Kimmeridgian. C. supremus would have primarily occurred during the Tithonian, at the very top of the Morrison Formation.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the proposed chronological succession of Camarasaurus species is accurate due to uncertainties in the relative dating of localities.
facts.quote: In 2017, Woodruff and Foster cautioned that the relative dating of the different localities within the Morrison Formation is still uncertain, which could undermine this proposed succession of species.

facts.statement: The hypothesis that Camarasaurus was semiaquatic was refuted in the 1970s, and it is now thought to have been entirely terrestrial.
facts.quote: The hypothesis of a semiaquatic lifestyle was refuted in the 1970s, when paleontologists such as Robert T. Bakker and Walter Coombs showed that the skeleton was not adapted for swimming, and that the teeth of Camarasaurus and Pelorosaurus must have processed coarse vegetation rather than water plants, amongst other lines of evidence. Sauropods are now thought to have been entirely terrestrial.

facts.statement: The genus Camarasaurus was established by Cope in 1877.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Cope, 1877

facts.statement: The type species of Camarasaurus is C. supremus.
facts.quote: type_species: Camarasaurus supremus

facts.statement: Camarasaurus lived during the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Jurásico Superior

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was the most common giant sauropod found in the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: Era un dinosaurio cuadrúpedo y herbívoro, el más común de los saurópodos gigantes encontrado en la Formación Morrison.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus lived during the late Jurassic period, approximately 155 to 145 million years ago, in what is now North America and France.
facts.quote: vivieron a finales del período Jurásico, hace aproximadamente 155 y 145 millones de años, en el Kimmeridgiense y el Titoniense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica y Francia.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus is a genus of three known species of camarasaurid sauropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus (gr. "lagarto de cámaras") es un género con tres especies conocidas de dinosaurios saurópodos camarasáuridos

facts.statement: The name Camarasaurus refers to hollows in the vertebrae and comes from Greek words meaning "chamber" and "lizard".
facts.quote: Su nombre se refiere a los huecos en las vértebras y proviene del griego καμαρα/kamara que significa "cámara", o cualquier cosa con una cubierta arqueada, y σαυρος/sauros que significa "lagarto".

facts.statement: Many complete skeletons of Camarasaurus have been recovered from Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming, and the Angeac-Charente excavation in France.
facts.quote: Ha habido un gran número de esqueletos completos recuperados en Colorado, Nuevo México, Utah y Wyoming y en la excavación de Angeac-Charente (Francia).

facts.statement: The three valid species of Camarasaurus are C. supremus, C. grandis, and C. lentus.
facts.quote: Las tres consideradas válidas son Camarasaurus supremus, Camarasaurus grandis y Camarasaurus lentus.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus had much thicker bones than Diplodocus, making it heavier despite having chambers that reduced spinal weight.
facts.quote: Los huesos de este gran herbívoro eran mucho más gruesos que los del Diplodocus, por lo que era más pesado a pesar de tener cámaras que reducían el peso de la columna vertebral.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus likely could not stand on its hind legs because its thick bones and large front limbs made the front of its body too heavy to lift.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus probablemente no podía pararse en sus patas traseras ya que los huesos más gruesos y las grandes extremidades delanteras indicaban que la parte frontal del cuerpo era demasiado pesada para poder levantarla del suelo.

facts.statement: The maximum size of the most common species, C. lentus, was about 15 meters in length.
facts.quote: El tamaño máximo de la especie más común, C. lentus, era de unos 15 metros de longitud.

facts.statement: The largest species, C. supremus, reached a maximum length of 23 meters and an estimated maximum weight of 47 tons.
facts.quote: La especie más grande, C. supremus, alcanzó una longitud máxima de 23 metros y un peso máximo estimado de 47 toneladas.

facts.statement: The arched skull of Camarasaurus was notably square with a blunt snout containing many fenestrae, and it is frequently recovered in good condition.
facts.quote: El cráneo arqueado de Camarasaurus era notablemente cuadrado y el hocico embotado tenía muchas fenestras, aunque era robusto y es recuperado con frecuencia en buenas condiciones por los paleontólogos.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus had 19-centimeter-long chisel-shaped teeth placed uniformly along the jaw.
facts.quote: Los dientes de 19 centímetros de largo tenían forma de cinceles y estaban colocados uniformemente a lo largo de la quijada.

facts.statement: The strength of its teeth indicates that Camarasaurus likely ate harder plant material than diplodocids with thin teeth.
facts.quote: La fuerza de los dientes indica que Camarasaurus comió probablemente un material vegetal más duro que los diplodócidos de dientes delgados.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus lived in open conifer forests where hard-edible plants were abundant.
facts.quote: Vivía en bosques de coníferas abiertos donde se encontraban por doquier plantas alimenticias duras.

facts.statement: Scientists previously suggested that Camarasaurus and other sauropods may have swallowed gastroliths to help grind food in the stomach, regurgitating them when they became too smooth.
facts.quote: Anteriormente, los científicos han sugerido que Camarasaurus y otros saurópodos pueden haber tragado gastrolitos, piedras, para ayudar a triturar los alimentos en el estómago, regurgitándolos cuando se volvían demasiado lisos.

facts.statement: A more recent analysis of stomach stone evidence suggests that Camarasaurus did not use gastroliths to grind food.
facts.quote: Un análisis más reciente, sin embargo, de la evidencia de las piedras del estómago sugiere que este no fue el caso.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus had stronger and more developed teeth than most sauropods, replaced on average every 62 days, indicating it could chew food to some extent before swallowing.
facts.quote: Los dientes fuertes y robustos de Camarasaurus estaban más desarrollados que los de la mayoría de los saurópodos y eran reemplazados en promedio cada 62 días, lo que indica que Camarasaurus pudo masticar los alimentos en su boca hasta cierto grado antes de tragar.

facts.statement: Other findings indicate that Camarasaurus preferred different vegetation than other sauropods, allowing them to share the same habitat without competition.
facts.quote: Otros hallazgos indican que Camarasaurus prefería vegetación diferente de la de otros saurópodos, Permitiéndoles compartir el mismo hábitat sin competir.

facts.statement: Fossilized remains along the jawline indicate that Camarasaurus had deep teeth covered by gums, with only the tips of the crowns protruding.
facts.quote: A lo largo de la línea de la mandíbula, los restos osificados de lo que parecen haber sido las encías del animal se han recuperado, lo que indica que Camarasaurus tenía dientes profundos cubiertos por las encías, con sólo las puntas de las coronas sobresaliendo.

facts.statement: Examinations suggest Camarasaurus teeth were covered by hard external scales and possibly a beak of some kind, though this is not certain.
facts.quote: Los exámenes de la muestra también indican que los dientes estaban cubiertos por duras escamas externas y posiblemente un pico de algún tipo, aunque esto no se sabe con certeza.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus feet had five toes each, with the inner toe having a large sharp claw for self-defense.
facts.quote: Los pies del Camarasaurus tenían cinco dedos cada uno, con el dedo del pie interno con una garra afilada grande para la autodefensa.

facts.statement: Like most sauropods, Camarasaurus had shorter front legs than back legs, but high shoulder placement made its back relatively flat.
facts.quote: Como la mayoría de los saurópodos, las patas delanteras eran más cortas que las traseras, pero la alta posición de los hombros hacia que la espalda fuera relativamente plana.

facts.statement: Like a modern elephant, Camarasaurus likely had a wedge of spongy tissue at the heel base to support its massive weight.
facts.quote: Como un elefante moderno, Camarasaurus parece haber tenido una cuña de tejido esponjoso en la base del talón, para apoyar el peso de una criatura tan grande.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus had shorter necks and tails than typically seen in sauropods of its size.
facts.quote: El cuello y la cola eran más cortos que lo que generalmente se ve en saurópodos de este tamaño.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus vertebrae were specialized for weight saving, with many being hollow or pneumatic, a feature seen in other sauropods.
facts.quote: Las vértebras fueron especializadas, respondiendo al propósito del ahorro de peso, según lo visto en muchos saurópodos posteriores, algunas de las vértebras eran ahuecadas, sirviendo para ahorrar peso, como se ve en otros saurópodos, muchas de las vértebras fueron ahuecadas o neumáticas.

facts.statement: The hollow vertebrae structure was poorly understood when Camarasaurus was discovered but inspired its name, meaning "chamber lizard".
facts.quote: Esta característica fue poco entendida en el momento de que Camarasaurus fuera descubierto, pero su estructura fue la inspiración para el nombre de la criatura, que significa "lagarto de cámara".

facts.statement: The absence of long upward projections on the spine suggests Camarasaurus could not stand on its hind legs.
facts.quote: La ausencia de tales estructuras de la espina dorsal de Camarasaurus sugiere que no pudiera levantarse en sus patas traseras.

facts.statement: Like other sauropods, Camarasaurus had a spinal cord swelling near the hips.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus, como otros saurópodos, tenía un abultamiento de la médula espinal cerca de las caderas.

facts.statement: Paleontologists originally believed the spinal cord swelling was a second brain, but modern opinion suggests it was likely a large area of nervous reflex activity rather than a brain.
facts.quote: Los paleontólogos creyeron originalmente esto era un segundo cerebro, quizás necesario para coordinar a una criatura tan enorme. La opinión moderna afirma que, mientras que pudo haber sido un área de actividad refleja nerviosa grande, no un cerebro.

facts.statement: The first Camarasaurus fossils, consisting of scattered vertebrae, were found in Colorado, USA, by Oramel W. Lucas.
facts.quote: Los primeros fósiles de Camarasaurus fueron hallados en Colorado, Estados Unidos, unas pocas vértebras dispersas fueron localizadas en Colorado, por Oramel W. Lucas.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877.
facts.quote: Fue nombrado por Edward Drinker Cope rápidamente en 1877.

facts.statement: Charles Gilmore discovered the first complete Camarasaurus skeleton in North America in 1925.
facts.quote: No fue hasta 1925, el año en que Charles Gilmore encontró el primer esqueleto completo del Camarasaurus en Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Other described species include C. grandis (1877), C. lentus (1889), and C. lewisi, originally described as the genus Cathetosaurus in 1988.
facts.quote: Otras especies descubiertas incluyen C. grandis, que significa gran lagarto de cámara, de 1877, C. lentus en 1889 y C. lewisi, originalmente descrito como un nuevo género Cathetosaurus, en 1988.

facts.statement: A 2013 analysis re-divided the genera of Camarasaurus and Cathetosaurus.
facts.quote: un análisis de 2013 dividió a los dos géneros nuevamente.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus lived from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian stages, between 161.5 and 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Oxfordian to Tithonian (161.5 to 143.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: C. supremus is the largest known species of Camarasaurus and one of the most massive sauropods known from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: C. supremo, como su nombre indica, es la especie más grande conocida de Camarasaurus y uno de los saurópodos más masivos conocidos de la Formación Morrison del jurásico tardío.

facts.statement: C. grandis is the oldest species and is found in the lowest rock layers of the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: C. grandis es la especie más antigua y se produjo en las capas de roca más bajas de la Formación Morrison.

facts.statement: C. lentus appeared later and coexisted with C. grandis for millions of years, possibly due to different ecological niches suggested by differences in their spinal anatomy.
facts.quote: C. lentus apareció más tarde, coexistiendo con C. grandis durante varios millones de años, posiblemente debido a diferentes nichos ecológicos como lo sugieren las diferencias en la anatomía espinal de las dos especies.

facts.statement: The immediate succession of species and their close similarity suggest that C. supremus may have evolved directly from C. lentus as a population of larger animals that survived later.
facts.quote: Esta sucesión inmediata de especies, así como la similitud muy estrecha entre las dos, sugiere que C. supremus puede haber evolucionado directamente de C. lentus, representando una población de animales más grandes, que sobrevivió más tarde.

facts.statement: During the Bone Wars, Othniel Charles Marsh named Morosaurus grandis, but most paleontologists now consider it a synonym of Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Más adelante durante la Guerra de los Huesos, Othniel Charles Marsh nombró al Morosaurus grandis, pero, la mayoría de los paleontólogos lo consideran actualmente un sinónimo de Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: Senter (2026) presents evidence regarding the limited range of motion of the fingers of Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Evidence of limited range of motion of fingers of Camarasaurus and Stegosaurus is presented by Senter (2026).

facts.statement: Carpenter, Ikejiri, and Wilson (2026) studied the postcranial skeletons of two immature Camarasaurus lentus specimens from the Morrison Formation in Utah, interpreting them as sequential ontogenetic stages to reveal morphological variability.
facts.quote: Carpenter, Ikejiri & Wilson (2026) study the anatomy of postcranial skeleton of two immature specimens of Camarasaurus lentus from the strata of the Morrison Formation from Dinosaur National Monument (Utah, United States), interpreted as representing sequential stages in the ontogeny of the species and providing new information on its morphological variability.
